venues.name: Café de Flore
venues.description: The beating heart of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, this legendary art deco café has hosted Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Picasso since 1887. Order a café crème and croissant at a sidewalk table to watch the world's most stylish pedestrian parade.

venues.name: Le Comptoir du Relais
venues.description: Chef Yves Camdeborde's impossibly cozy Saint-Germain bistro delivers market-fresh French classics to a packed house of devoted regulars and lucky tourists who scored one of Paris's hardest reservations. The weekend prix-fixe tasting menu is a love letter to traditional brasserie cooking.

venues.name: Cravan
venues.description: Paris's largest cocktail bar sprawls across a 17th-century building on the Boulevard Saint-Germain, drawing night owls with an inventive list that includes the house signature: Champagne spiked with immortelle extract. Mushroom tempura and black-garlic dipping sauce keep the crowd anchored until 2am weekends.

venues.name: Rex Club
venues.description: The spiritual home of French techno since 1990, the Rex Club's legendary sound system and resident DJs including Laurent Garnier have made its basement dance floor a pilgrimage site for electronic music devotees worldwide. Don't arrive before midnight if you want to feel the room reach critical mass.

venues.name: Breizh Café
venues.description: This acclaimed Breton crêperie in the Marais has revolutionized the humble galette with premium organic buckwheat batter filled with seasonal ingredients like smoked salmon roe and crème fraîche, earning a cult following among food-obsessed Parisians. Pair a savory galette with the remarkable natural cider selection.

venues.name: Géosmine
venues.description: Chef Maxime Bouttier's duplex restaurant in a converted 11th arrondissement textile factory serves hyper-seasonal French tasting menus where artichoke braised in white wine arrives wrapped in ribbons of lardo, and every dish carries the philosophy of its name — the smell of freshly turned earth. One of Paris's most exciting young restaurants right now.
venues.address: 71 Rue de La Folie Méricourt, 75011 Paris

venues.name: Le Baron
venues.description: The longtime anchor of Paris's exclusive club scene, Le Baron in the 8th arrondissement continues to draw a fashion-forward international crowd to its discreetly signed red-velvet lounge where the guest list policy is famously strict. A genuinely Parisian night out where celebrities, models, and DJs collide on a small but electric dance floor.

venues.name: Septime
venues.description: Consistently ranked among Europe's 50 best restaurants, Bertrand Grébaut's Bastille neo-bistro serves ingredient-led, natural-wine-paired tasting menus that feel simultaneously simple and revelatory — think raw shrimp with fermented rice cream and shiso, or milk-fed lamb with seasonal grains. Booking opens monthly and disappears within minutes.

venues.name: Le Syndicat
venues.description: A proudly nationalist cocktail bar that uses exclusively French spirits — no Scotch, no Bourbon — crafting inventive drinks from Calvados, Cognac, Armagnac, and artisan French gins in a cramped, graffiti-lined space in the 10th arrondissement. The bar that proved France doesn't need imports to make world-class cocktails.

venues.name: Café Procope
venues.description: Established in 1686 and reportedly the world's oldest café still in operation, Procope in Saint-Germain served Voltaire, Rousseau, and Napoleon Bonaparte — whose hat remains in a glass case upstairs. Today it functions as a full French brasserie, but the historic gilded interior and literary mythology make every coffee feel consequential.

venues.name: Café du Turin
venues.description: The undisputed institution for seafood aperitifs on the Place Garibaldi, Café du Turin has been shucking the finest oysters and sea urchins on the Côte d'Azur since 1908. Arrive at noon for a dozen Fines de Claires and a cold Provençal rosé before the crowds descend.

venues.name: Jan Restaurant
venues.description: South African chef Jan Hendrik van der Westhuizen brings the flavors of his homeland to the Côte d'Azur, weaving Cape Malay spices and South African wines into a Michelin-starred tasting menu that feels utterly original in the heart of the French Riviera. The terrace overlooking Nice's ochre rooftops is a dream backdrop.

venues.name: Bar des Oiseaux
venues.description: Tucked on a narrow medieval lane in Vieux-Nice, this warmly lit natural wine bar draws a knowledgeable local crowd with an ever-changing list of small-producer bottles from Corsica, Provence, and beyond. Small plates of charcuterie and Niçoise cheese make it easy to linger through the evening.

venues.name: Chez Pipo
venues.description: The definitive address for socca — Nice's beloved chickpea pancake — Chez Pipo has been making the city's best version in a wood-fired oven since 1923, serving it scorching hot on brown paper with zero frills and maximum flavor. This is the original, the others are imitations.

venues.name: L'Effervescence
venues.description: The Riviera's most respected club for electronic music hosts an internationally curated DJ lineup across two floors of a refurbished venue near the train station, drawing a discerning crowd of Nice locals and well-traveled party tourists. The sound system is legitimately exceptional.

venues.name: Babel Babel
venues.description: A buzzy Mediterranean small-plates restaurant in the hip Libération neighborhood that perfectly channels Nice's multicultural soul, serving mezze-style dishes rooted in Niçoise, Lebanese, and Maghrebi cooking. The vine-covered terrace and natural-wine list make every visit feel like a discovery.

venues.name: La Cave du Fromager
venues.description: A subterranean wine and cheese bar carved into the medieval foundations of Vieux-Nice, offering one of the most intimate aperitif experiences on the Côte d'Azur. The staff's encyclopedic knowledge of Provençal wines paired with aged Comté and fresh chèvre makes this a genuinely instructive pit-stop.

venues.name: Le Plongeoir
venues.description: Perched on a rock platform jutting into the sea off Cap de Nice with views stretching to the Alps, this iconic dining platform built around a 1930s diving board serves fresh Mediterranean seafood and rosé to one of the most spectacular outdoor dining crowds in France. You don't eat here for the food alone — the setting is the whole point.

venues.name: Ruban Bleu
venues.description: A beloved Promenade des Anglais institution known for its front-row sea views, all-day café menu, and classic pan bagnat — the great Niçoise sandwich of tuna, olives, and egg on olive-oil-soaked bread. The terrace at golden hour with the Mediterranean stretching in every direction is an unforgettable Riviera snapshot.

venues.name: Le Smarties
venues.description: Nice's longest-running LGBTQ+ club in the heart of the old town parties hard three nights a week with pop, house, and drag nights that draw an inclusive, high-energy mix of locals, expats, and tourists. The best club in Nice for anyone who wants to actually dance rather than pose.

venues.name: Café des Fédérations
venues.description: The most authentic bouchon lyonnais in the city, with its red-checked tablecloths, shared benches, and a fixed four-course menu that hasn't deviated from andouillette and quenelle in forty years. Every Lyonnais you ask will claim it's a tourist trap, then admit they go anyway because the food is just that good.

venues.name: Le Dôme Bar
venues.description: Housed inside a converted 19th-century chapel with a 32-meter-high painted dome, this theatrical cocktail bar in the heart of Lyon's Presqu'île is one of the most visually arresting drinking spaces in France. The baroque grandeur contrasts brilliantly with the modern cocktail menu.

venues.name: Paul Bocuse Brasserie Nord
venues.description: The Art Deco brasserie bearing the legendary chef's name serves his most accessible menu — roast chicken, Lyon sausage with lentils, and impeccable tarte tatin — in a magnificent 1930s dining room that was once a railway café. An essential Lyon experience that's surprisingly democratic in price.

venues.name: Hot Club de Lyon
venues.description: One of Europe's oldest jazz clubs, founded in 1948, the Hot Club continues its mission in a vaulted stone cellar in Vieux Lyon where live bebop, swing, and contemporary jazz fill the underground space every night except Monday. The quintessential Lyon music experience.

venues.name: Café Comptoir Abel
venues.description: A family-run bouchon that opened in 1928 and shows absolutely no sign of modernizing — and that's the entire point. The quenelle de brochet with Nantua sauce here is the platonic ideal of the dish, and the house Beaujolais is poured generously from terracotta pots called pots lyonnais. Arrive hungry and with time.

venues.name: Ninkasi Gerland
venues.description: Lyon's beloved homegrown craft brewery and bar-restaurant complex in the Gerland district pours eight house-brewed beers on tap in a cavernous industrial-chic space that also hosts live music and cinema nights. The terrace in summer becomes the city's most democratic meeting point.

venues.name: Le Sucre
venues.description: Lyon's crown jewel of electronic music occupies the extraordinary rooftop of a 1930s sugar refinery — La Sucrière — and hosts touring international DJs under the open sky with a panoramic view over the Rhône and the city's illuminated skyline. One of Europe's great outdoor club venues.

venues.name: Takao Takano
venues.description: Japanese-born chef Takao Takano distills the soul of Lyon's market gardens into a Michelin-starred tasting menu that has no menu at all — he cooks exclusively what the season and his instinct dictate. The 12-seat room at the edge of the 6th arrondissement feels like being invited into a chef's private kitchen.

venues.name: Café 203
venues.description: A compact, perpetually buzzing neobistro-café in the trendy 1st arrondissement that serves excellent espresso beside inventive seasonal tartines and natural wine from 8am well into the night. Lyon's creative class uses it as an unofficial headquarters.

venues.name: Brasserie Georges
venues.description: Founded in 1836 and still going strong, this cathedral-like Belle Époque brasserie seats 500 guests under its magnificent painted ceilings and has been brewing its own lager on the premises for nearly two centuries. Order the choucroute royale and a glass of the house beer in one of Lyon's most breathtaking dining rooms.

venues.name: Bar à Vin - CIVB
venues.description: The official wine bar of the Bordeaux wine trade council occupies a 16th-century building opposite the Grand Théâtre, pouring sixty different Bordeaux wines by the glass at remarkably democratic prices. This is where wine buyers, sommeliers, and curious travelers all sit side by side at the curved oak bar.

venues.name: Le Pressoir d'Argent Gordon Ramsay
venues.description: Gordon Ramsay's two-Michelin-star Bordeaux outpost inside the Grand Hotel delivers the most theatrically French fine dining experience in the city — including a 150-year-old silver wine press that tables can use to press their own Sauternes-paired dessert course. The wine pairings emphasize local terroir with remarkable depth.

venues.name: Soif
venues.description: A lovingly curated natural wine bar with a 35-bottle-strong list built around small producers from the Gironde and across France, serving market-inspired small plates alongside glasses that represent the best of contemporary winemaking. The ground-floor room is tiny, so arrive early or grab a street-side perch.

venues.name: Café du Port
venues.description: A riverside café with an unbeatable terrace overlooking the Garonne and the Pont de Pierre, where Bordelais locals gather for morning coffee and afternoon wine in equal measure. The relaxed atmosphere and excellent croque-monsieur make it the city's best spot for people-watching along the riverbank.

venues.name: Symbiose
venues.description: A contemporary small-plates bistro whose street-level dining room leads through a hidden doorway into a speakeasy-style cocktail bar — making it one of Bordeaux's most cleverly conceived evening destinations. Chef Antoine Adeiran's seasonal dishes are honest and delicious before the cocktail chapter begins.

venues.name: Le Bootlegger
venues.description: Bordeaux's best rock and indie club is a sweat-soaked basement venue near the Saint-Pierre quarter that books international touring bands alongside local acts, keeping the city's live music scene honest and unpretentious. The bar is cheap, the crowd is passionate, and no one is there to be seen.

venues.name: La Brasserie Bordelaise
venues.description: A temple of Aquitaine beef and Bordelaise bone marrow served in a handsome tiled dining room by the covered market of the Capucins, this restaurant makes the case that Bordeaux's cuisine is just as exceptional as its wine. The entrecôte à la bordelaise — grilled rib-eye with shallot and marrow sauce — is the dish to order.

venues.name: Mama Shelter Bordeaux
venues.description: The rooftop bar of the hip Mama Shelter hotel in the Saint-Paul district serves cocktails and pintxos to a terraced crowd that feels more like a house party than a hotel bar. DJ sets most weekends and a brilliant view of the Grosse Cloche bell tower make it a reliably excellent Bordeaux night out.

venues.name: La Tête de Bœuf
venues.description: A quintessential neighborhood café-tabac in the working-class Bastide district on the right bank, where builders, office workers, and visiting journalists share zinc bar stools for a tartine and a café serré at 7am. The unchanged 1950s décor, €2.20 coffee, and complete lack of tourism make it one of the city's most authentic spaces.

venues.name: IBoat
venues.description: A converted barge moored on the Garonne that functions as Bordeaux's most beloved cultural club — part concert hall, part outdoor terrace, part techno bunker — hosting everything from reggae to minimal techno across its multiple decks. The setting is absolutely unique and the programming punches well above its weight for a city this size.

venues.name: La Mercerie
venues.description: London chef Harry Cummins and Montreal sommelier Laura Vidal created Marseille's most internationally celebrated restaurant in a converted textile factory in the Cours Julien neighborhood — a five-course dinner of precise, herb-driven French cooking paired with Laura's natural wine selection is one of the best meals in southern France.

venues.name: Figure Wine Bar
venues.description: A powder-pink natural wine bar in the Vauban neighborhood that has single-handedly elevated the area's dining scene, buzzing from the moment the sun comes out with small plates of tarama with green oil, gorgonzola with apricots, and impeccably crisped pommes dauphine. The terrace is an unstoppable magnet on warm evenings.

venues.name: Pizzéria Chez Sauveur
venues.description: Open since 1943 and making Neapolitan-descended pizza with a thin, crackling crust across 18 topping options in a dimly lit dining room on a narrow old-town street — La Spéciale, finished post-bake with cherry tomatoes, olives, and pistou (Provençal pesto without the nuts), is a Marseille classic that never disappoints.

venues.name: Bar de la Marine
venues.description: Marcel Pagnol set his Marius trilogy in this exact waterfront bar on the Vieux-Port, and the wooden interior, zinc bar, and pastis-drinking fishermen have barely changed since the 1930s. A glass of pastis here while watching boats navigate the old harbor is as Marseille as it gets.

venues.name: AM par Alexandre Mazzia
venues.description: Three-Michelin-star chef Alexandre Mazzia—born in the Congo, raised in Marseille—delivers arguably the most ambitious and personal tasting menu in France from a small, intimate room in the 8th arrondissement, where Congolese memory, Provençal produce, and technical wizardry combine into something utterly unlike any other restaurant in the country.

venues.name: Café de l'Abbaye
venues.description: An ancient stone café tucked against the walls of the Saint-Victor Basilica in the 7th arrondissement, serving strong Corsican coffee and almond tarts to a mix of local residents and pilgrims who've been climbing this hill since the 5th century. One of Marseille's most charming and unhurried terraces.

venues.name: Le Trolleybus
venues.description: Marseille's most storied superclub occupies a series of converted tram depots near the Vieux-Port and spreads across five rooms of house, techno, and R&B nightly, pulling the city's most diverse and high-energy crowd. The outdoor terrace between the rooms gives the whole place an almost carnival atmosphere in summer.

venues.name: La Boîte à Sardine
venues.description: The best standing-room-only fish counter in Marseille sources entirely from the day's catch at the adjacent Vieux-Port fish market, serving the freshest sea urchin, grilled red mullet, and bouillabaisse portions to a tightly packed lunchtime crowd that knows what it's there for. Cash only, arrive early, eat standing.

venues.name: Ventre Saint-Gris
venues.description: A compact, low-lit cocktail bar in the Cours Julien arts district that makes a remarkable case for Provençal herbs and spirits in its cocktail recipes — lavender-infused pastis sours, Corsican myrtle liqueur negronis — drawing a creative neighborhood crowd who treat it as their unofficial living room.
venues.address: 16 Place Notre Dame du Mont, 13006 Marseille

venues.name: Café La Caravelle
venues.description: Perched above the Vieux-Port in a 17th-century building that once housed the Hôtel de Ville tax office, La Caravelle's mezzanine terrace delivers one of the finest harbor views in Europe alongside excellent coffee, Ricard, and jazz on weekend evenings. The ceiling is covered in ship models from across the centuries.

venues.name: Café Gijón
venues.description: A literary café in continuous operation since 1888 on the Paseo de Recoletos, Café Gijón has hosted Lorca, Hemingway, and every important Spanish intellectual of the 20th century at its marble-topped tables. Order a café con leche and a tostada con tomate and settle into the timeless dark-wood interior.

venues.name: DiverXO
venues.description: David Muñoz's three-Michelin-star spectacle is the most extravagant restaurant in Spain — a roving 30-course tasting journey through Asian-Spanish flavors served by a troupe of theatrical staff in a room of chinoiserie excess inside the NH Collection Eurobuilding. Booking opens a month in advance and sells out in minutes.

venues.name: 1862 Dry Bar
venues.description: A narrow, Victorian-appointed cocktail bar in the Malasaña district where the drinks menu reads like a 19th-century pharmacopoeia — bitters-forward, spirit-led, and impeccably made. The tight space and knowledgeable bartenders make it one of Madrid's best places to have a proper conversation over a well-crafted drink.

venues.name: Sala El Sol
venues.description: The club that launched La Movida Madrileña — the post-Franco cultural explosion — Sala El Sol has been Madrid's most historically significant music venue since 1979, hosting everyone from Mecano and Alaska to international indie acts in its intimate subterranean room. The nostalgia here isn't kitsch; it's real.

venues.name: Taberna La Carmencita
venues.description: Founded in 1854 and retaining every scrap of its original ceramic tiles, marble bar, and wooden partitions, La Carmencita in Chueca is the city's most beautiful and genuinely old taberna, serving cocido madrileño, tortilla, and house-made croquetas to regulars who've been coming for generations. Hemingway's name is in the archive.

venues.name: Angelita Madrid
venues.description: A four-floor natural wine bar and vermouth house in Malasaña that covers every base from morning vermut on the terrace to late-night natural wine in the candlelit basement — one of Madrid's most complete drinking establishments. The natural wine list is one of the best-curated in Spain.

venues.name: Lateral Gran Vía
venues.description: A modern tapas bar with a rooftop terrace facing the Gran Vía that does exactly what Madrid's best mid-range restaurants do — serves generous, reliable croquetas, patatas bravas, and jamón ibérico to a mix of locals and tourists who want decent food at a fair price in a central location. No pretension, just pleasure.

venues.name: Café Comercial
venues.description: Madrid's oldest café (1887) in the Bilbao neighborhood, lovingly restored to its original mirrored grandeur after a decade-long closure, now serves excellent cortados and weekend vermouth to a new generation of locals in an impossibly beautiful Belle Époque setting. The chess club meets on Tuesday evenings.

venues.name: Corral de la Morería
venues.description: The world's oldest and most decorated flamenco tablao (open since 1956) stages nightly performances by top-tier dancers, guitarists, and cantaores in an intimate candlelit room in the La Latina neighborhood, pairing the art with an optional Michelin-starred tasting menu. A genuinely moving live music experience.

venues.name: StreetXO
venues.description: David Muñoz's street-food alter ego takes place in a punk-rock open kitchen in El Corte Inglés de Castellana — 30-seat counter dining where you watch the chaos of Asian-Spanish street food being cooked at full volume in front of you, and the spiced pork taco with smoked eel mayo is as good as high-end food gets at this price point.

venues.name: El Xampanyet
venues.description: A tile-clad cava bar in the El Born neighborhood that has been pouring house cava and anchovies on bread since 1929, filling its few marble-topped tables with the most convivial pre-dinner crowd in Barcelona. The house cava — poured into saucers not flutes — costs less than a coffee at any nearby hotel.

venues.name: Bodega Sepúlveda
venues.description: A wood-paneled neighborhood tavern in the Eixample dating to 1921 that serves vermouth, anchovies, and honest Catalan cooking to a fiercely loyal local clientele — the kind of place that has never needed a website and never will. The butifarra sausage with mongetes beans is a Barcelona essential.

venues.name: Nomad Coffee Lab
venues.description: Spain's most internationally acclaimed specialty coffee roastery operates this compact tasting room and café in the Raval neighborhood, where single-origin pour-overs and perfectly pulled ristrettos are served with the same seriousness applied in Nordic coffee culture — but with unmistakably Spanish warmth.

venues.name: Ático by Ramon Freixa
venues.description: The two-Michelin-star penthouse restaurant of the El Palace Hotel gives the city's most cinematic dining experience — floor-to-ceiling views of the Eixample grid at night while chef Ramon Freixa serves his technically brilliant Catalan-accented tasting menus. The rooftop terrace aperitif is worth the price of admission alone.
venues.address: Gran Via de les Corts Catalanes, 668, 08010 Barcelona

venues.name: Garage Beer Co.
venues.description: Barcelona's pioneering craft brewery turned its modest Eixample taproom into the city's most influential beer venue — pouring 20 taps of house-brewed IPAs, lagers, and stouts alongside a guest beer program that brings in the best European producers. Bare concrete, good music, and serious beer at sensible prices.
venues.address: Carrer del Consell de Cent, 261, 08011 Barcelona

venues.name: Razzmatazz
venues.description: Five rooms, five simultaneous music policies — from indie rock to techno — make this converted warehouse in Poblenou the most comprehensive club in Spain, hosting everyone from Arctic Monkeys to Richie Hawtin since 2000. The sheer scale of the party ensures every musical tribe finds its room.

venues.name: Bar Calders
venues.description: The self-appointed king of the Sant Antoni neighborhood's vibrant vermouth scene occupies a prime corner terrace where young Barcelonins gather on Sunday mornings for vermouth, house-made potato chips, and the ritual that defines Catalan social life. No reservations, no concept — just the best vermut in the city.

venues.name: Enigma
venues.description: Albert Adrià's theatrical six-act tasting menu takes place over 40+ courses in a futuristic white labyrinth beneath the Eixample streets, guiding diners through zones of temperature, texture, and flavor with the conceptual rigor you'd expect from the brother of Ferran. Booking opens weeks in advance at a specific hour; set an alarm.

venues.name: El Nacional
venues.description: A magnificent 1920s Art Deco pavilion near the Passeig de Gràcia that houses four restaurants, two bars, and a market hall simultaneously — offering everything from a coffee at the marble bar to a full paella in the covered courtyard. Barcelona's most impressive gathering place for food and drink.

venues.name: Otto Zutz
venues.description: Barcelona's most enduring upscale club has been a fixture of the Gràcia neighborhood's glittering nightlife since 1985, drawing a fashion-industry crowd to three floors of hip-hop, R&B, and house music in an industrial-chic warehouse. The queue on Friday is long but moves faster than the legend suggests.

venues.name: El Rinconcillo
venues.description: The oldest bar in Seville (founded 1670), its ancient marble counters and walls covered in jamón legs and dusty bottles have barely changed in three and a half centuries. Bartenders still chalk your tab on the bar top, the montaditos are sublime, and a cold manzanilla here connects you directly to the soul of Andalusia.

venues.name: ConTenedor
venues.description: An inventive slow-food restaurant in the Macarena neighborhood where organic, hyperlocal ingredients are plated like edible modern art — artisan beet tagliatelle with black olive cream, or seasonal mushrooms with apple-pepper sauce — at surprisingly honest prices after 18 years at the top of Seville's dining scene.

venues.name: Café de Indias
venues.description: A sun-drenched art-colonial café inside the former Casa Lonja de Mercaderes — the same building that houses the Archivo de Indias — serving Seville's finest café cortado alongside traditional torrijas and bollos on a terrace watched over by orange trees. The architectural setting alone is worth the price of a coffee.

venues.name: Las Golondrinas
venues.description: A beloved no-frills Triana tapas bar with blue-and-white azulejo tiles, brisk bartenders, and exceptional champiñones (mushrooms in green alioli) and puntas de solomillo (grilled tenderloin on crispy chips) that make it a prime example of why Seville's working-class tapas culture is the best in Spain.

venues.name: La Carbonería
venues.description: A free-entry flamenco bar in a crumbling old coal merchant's warehouse in the Santa Cruz neighborhood that stages spontaneous and semi-organized flamenco shows nightly from around 11pm — no ticketing, no pretension, just passionate artists and a crowd that's half local, half fascinated tourist. The most authentic flamenco experience in Seville.

venues.name: Abades Triana
venues.description: A glass-walled fine dining room projecting over the Guadalquivir River in Triana with the most theatrical dining view in Seville — the illuminated Torre del Oro and Cathedral skyline reflected in the water below. The Andalusian seafood and rice dishes are excellent, but the panoramic terrace is transformative at sunset.

venues.name: La Terraza de EME
venues.description: A rooftop cocktail bar with cathedral views — specifically the Giralda tower rising impossibly close above you — at the boutique EME Catedral Hotel in the Santa Cruz quarter. Drinking a fino sherry cocktail as the Moorish tower glows golden at dusk is one of Seville's most indulgent pleasures.

venues.name: Bar La Fresquita
venues.description: A legendary no-sign dive bar in the Feria neighborhood where the entire block socializes over tinto de verano and papas aliñadas on plastic chairs dragged into the narrow street, typifying the informal Sevillian outdoor bar culture that no amount of tourist development has managed to sanitize.

venues.name: Lalola de Javi Abascal
venues.description: Chef Javier Abascal's fine dining inside the whitewashed internal courtyard of a 16th-century palace turned boutique hotel delivers elevated Iberian cooking — Presa Ibérica, offal preparations, and ceviches — that feels simultaneously rooted in Andalusian tradition and in genuine creative dialogue with contemporary cooking.

venues.name: Café Central
venues.description: Seville's most charming outdoor café tables spill across the shaded Plaza del Salvador in the historic center, making it the city's prime morning café-con-leche spot after the fish market vendors and before the tourist tide — the churros here are as good as they come in Andalusia, and the locals who've been coming for decades will tell you so.

venues.name: Casa Montaña
venues.description: A century-old wine tavern in the Cabanyal beach neighborhood whose walls are covered in dusty old barrels and whose wine list spans 800 natural and traditional labels — this is where Valencia's most knowledgeable wine lovers gather for clóchinas (local mussels), patatas bravas, and bottles you won't find anywhere else in the city.

venues.name: Central Bar (Mercado Central)
venues.description: Inside Valencia's magnificent Art Nouveau covered market, chef Ricard Camarena operates a counter that serves the best almuerzo (mid-morning brunch) in the city — house-made embutidos on a rosca roll, oysters from the counter, and a cold cerveza — all sourced from the stalls surrounding you in one of Europe's finest food markets.
venues.address: Plaça de la Ciutat de Bruges, s/n, 46001 Valencia

venues.name: El Poblet
venues.description: Two Michelin stars and chef Luis Valls's mastery of Valencia's sacred rice dishes — served in a spare, elegant dining room near the City of Arts — make this the definitive destination for anyone who wants to understand why paella is a serious art form. The arroz a banda with lobster bisque is among the finest plates of food in Spain.

venues.name: L'Umbracle Terrazza
venues.description: A futuristic open-air club and bar set inside Calatrava's luminous L'Umbracle botanical walkway at the City of Arts and Sciences, mixing DJ sets with the surreal backdrop of Valencia's most iconic architecture. The outdoor terrace is extraordinary and summer nights here feel genuinely cinematic.
venues.address: Av. del Professor López Piñero, 5, 46013 Valencia

venues.name: Bar Ricardo
venues.description: A bustling Ruzafa neighborhood bar where locals pack three deep for weekday vermut and the weekend aperitivo ritual, sustained entirely by the best patatas bravas and house-made pickles in the city. No cocktails, no craft beer — just cold Estrella Damm, raw honesty, and the best aperitivo in Valencia.

venues.name: Café Infusiones
venues.description: A pioneering specialty coffee shop in the Ruzafa neighborhood that brought third-wave coffee culture to Valencia before it was fashionable, serving meticulous V60 pour-overs from rotating single-origin beans in a calm, plant-filled room that doubles as a workspace for half the neighborhood's freelancers.

venues.name: La Cantina de Ruzafa
venues.description: Ruzafa's most beloved neighborhood trattoria fuses Italian and Valencian pantry instincts into a daily changing menu of pasta, rice, and market vegetables that encapsulates what this eclectic multicultural neighborhood has become. Natural wines, no reservations, and a queue that starts forming at 20:00.

venues.name: Akuarela Playa
venues.description: A beachfront club on Malvarrosa Beach that defines Valencia's summer nightlife — dance floors open to the sea, sunrise DJ sets, and a crowd that arrives at 4am because the night hasn't started yet. The combination of sand under your feet and house music in the warm Mediterranean air is impossible to replicate anywhere else.
venues.address: Passeig Marítim de la Patacona, s/n, 46120 Alboraia

venues.name: Askua
venues.description: A serious steak and ember-grilled meat restaurant near the Palau de la Música that treats Galician beef with the reverence most cities reserve for premium sushi — the T-bones are aged 60+ days and arrive on custom slate boards with nothing but sea salt. Valencia's answer to the Basque steak temples of San Sebastián.

venues.name: Radio City Valencia
venues.description: A legendary multi-room cultural club in the Carmen historic quarter that hosts live music, flamenco, world music, and DJ nights across four stages with free entry before midnight — making it the best value nightlife experience in the city and an institution of Valencia's alternative cultural life since 1982.

venues.name: Bar Los Diamantes
venues.description: The definitive Granada tapas bar, where the city's sacred tradition of free tapas with every drink reaches its pinnacle — order a cold Alhambra beer and a mountain of fresh seafood appears gratis. The ceramic-tiled Plaza de la Pescadería original has been replicated but never surpassed.

venues.name: Tetería Al Faguara
venues.description: A Moorish-style teahouse in the Albaicín quarter where mint tea is poured from great heights into Moroccan glasses and shisha smoke curls through arched windows facing the Alhambra's towers — a direct descendant of the Nasrid civilization that shaped this city. The baklava and almond pastries are extraordinary.

venues.name: Restaurante Carmela
venues.description: A beloved Granadan institution in the Realejo neighborhood serving outstanding modern interpretations of Andalusian cuisine — the salmorejo, oxtail braised in Pedro Ximénez, and ajo blanco with Málaga grapes are all textbook perfect — to a loyal crowd of locals and discerning visitors who know the difference.

venues.name: El Bar de Eric
venues.description: A wine-focused bar in the Realejo neighborhood run by a Franco-Granadan couple that quietly became the city's best natural wine destination — a tiny room with 150 labels, excellent cheese, and an atmosphere of relaxed expertise that makes it the perfect counterpoint to Granada's tapas bar chaos.

venues.name: Granada 10
venues.description: A repurposed art-house cinema in the city center that transforms at midnight into Granada's most eclectic and genuinely fun nightclub — spinning Spanish pop, reggaeton, and '80s hits to a university-heavy crowd who dance until 5am on the same floors where generations of Granadans once watched films. Free entry before 1am.

venues.name: Mirador de Morayma
venues.description: A garden terrace restaurant carved into the hillside of the Albaicín with the most captivating Alhambra views in Granada, serving Granadan classics like habas con jamón and remojón oranges with cod alongside a wine list weighted toward Andalusian producers. Dining here at sunset is a genuinely emotional experience.

venues.name: Café Futbol
venues.description: Since 1930 this café on the Plaza de Mariana Pineda has been serving Granada's most acclaimed churros con chocolate — thicker and darker than the Madrid variety, the chocolate is practically molten ganache. A morning here watching the city wake up from a corner table is as close to perfect as breakfasts get.

venues.name: Cueva del Sacromonte La Zambra
venues.description: A genuine cave dwelling hewn from the limestone of the Sacromonte hillside that stages nightly zambra flamenco shows — the oldest and most private form of flamenco, originally performed by Granada's Romani community in candlelit grottoes. The whitewashed cave walls and the intimacy of the setting make this unlike any other flamenco experience.

venues.name: Taberna La Cueva de 1900
venues.description: A genuinely antique wine cellar in the university quarter that offers Granada's most immersive free-tapas experience — each round of drinks brings larger and more elaborate accompaniments, starting with olives and escalating to hot stews and meat preparations after a few rounds. The walls are pasted with yellowing bullfight posters.

venues.name: Damasqueros
venues.description: Chef Lola Marín's quiet Realejo restaurant has become Granada's most critically acclaimed modern dining destination — a tightly conceived four-course menu of Andalusian produce elevated with technique and genuine creativity, served in a converted historic house with an intimate dining room that feels like a particularly well-curated private home.
